This vignette walks through each step of the data preparation process, from
raw ROXAS / ROXAS AI output files to the files for a TRIA submission.

```{r setup, eval = FALSE}
library(rxs2tria)
```

# Step 1: Locate ROXAS files

Set the path to a folder containing the ROXAS or ROXAS AI output files
of your QWA dataset. Files may be organised in subdirectories.
`get_roxas_files()` checks that all required files are present for
each image and returns a data frame of their full file paths.

For **ROXAS**, the required files per image are:

- Cells output (`{IMAGEID}_Output_Cells.txt`)
- Rings output (`{IMAGEID}_Output_Rings.txt`)
- Settings file (`{IMAGEID}_ROXAS_Settings.txt`)
- Image file (`{IMAGEID}.jpg`; also `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.bmp`, `.tiff`)

For **ROXAS AI**, the required files per image are:

- Cells table (`{IMAGEID}.cells_table.csv` or `.txt`)
- Rings table (`{IMAGEID}.rings_table.csv` or `.txt`)
- Metadata file (`{IMAGEID}.metadata.json`)
- Image file (`{IMAGEID}.scan.jpg`; also `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.bmp`, `.tiff`)

```{r, eval = FALSE}
roxas_version <- "roxas" # or "roxas_ai"
path_in <- "path/to/ROXAS_data"
files <- get_roxas_files(path_in, roxas_version)
```


# Step 2: Extract the data structure

QWA data are organised hierarchically: each analysed *image* was taken
of a microsection/*slide*, each slide was cut from a *woodpiece* (e.g.
a core or a wedge), and each woodpiece was sampled from a *tree* of a 
certain *species* at a specific *site*. Typically, some or all of this 
information is encoded in the image file names.
[Fonti et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1505389) recommend
the naming convention:

`{site}_{species}_{tree/woodpiece}_{slide}_{image}`

e.g. `S22_LADE_L08b_1_2.jpg` is the second image of the first slide
from woodpiece *b* of the *Larix decidua* tree *L08* at site *S22*.

`extract_data_structure()` extracts this hierarchy using a regular
expression with
[named groups](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/articles/regular-expressions.html).
Each named group (`site`, `species`, `tree`, `woodpiece`, `slide`,
`image`) that appears in the pattern is extracted and used to construct
the full hierarchical labels. 
Not all groups need to be in the pattern:
If, for example, all images belong to the same site and/or species, the
`site_label` and/or `species_code` arguments can be supplied instead of
including `site`/`species` groups in the pattern. Or if each tree was cored
exactly once, there may not be a specific woodpiece identifier, and it 
can be left out of the pattern.

Adapt the pattern to match your naming convention using named regex groups.
Supported group names: site, species, tree, woodpiece, slide, image.
Example below assumes the common convention
  `{site}_{species}_{tree}_{slide}_{image}`
with alphanumeric components and one woodpiece per tree (no separate woodpiece
identifier). If your naming includes a woodpiece identifier, you can add it
 (e.g. by including "(?<woodpiece>[[:alnum:]]+)" between the tree and slide groups).
See the documentation of `extract_data_structure()` for more information.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pattern <- "(?<site>[[:alnum:]]+)_(?<species>[[:alnum:]]+)_(?<tree>[[:alnum:]]+)_(?<slide>[[:alnum:]]+)_(?<image>[[:alnum:]]+)"
df_structure <- extract_data_structure(files, pattern)

# or:
# pattern <- "(?<tree>[[:alnum:]]+)_(?<slide>[[:alnum:]]+)_(?<image>[[:alnum:]]+)"
# df_structure <- extract_data_structure(
#   files, pattern, site_label = "S22", species_code = "LADE")
```

**Always inspect the result** with `View(df_structure)` before
proceeding to confirm that all labels were extracted correctly and the
hierarchy is consistent.


# Step 3: Collect metadata

## From the ROXAS or ROXAS AI files

`collect_settings_data()` reads the per-image ROXAS settings (or ROXAS
AI metadata) and the image files: their EXIF data for classic ROXAS,
their actual file size for ROXAS AI. The result is combined with the data
structure from Step 2 into a `QWAimages` object using `build_QWAimages()`.

Passing the data structure directly, the ROXAS version is auto-detected
from the settings file names, and the image files are read from the
`fname_image` column.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df_settings <- collect_settings_data(df_structure)
```

Alternatively, the settings and image file paths can be supplied
individually, and the version can be set explicitly:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df_settings <- collect_settings_data(files_settings = df_structure$fname_settings,
                                     files_images = df_structure$fname_image,
                                     roxas_version = "roxas")
```

For classic ROXAS, `meas_created_at` is read as a raw character string,
as its format depends on the locale. Convert it explicitly to `POSIXct`
with the format(s) and timezone appropriate for your data, and address
any conversion warnings before overwriting the column in `df_settings`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# for ROXAS only (ROXAS AI has standardised timestamps, so already converted)
settings_date_orders <- c("%d.%m.%Y %H:%M:%S", "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M") # adjust to your locale
if (roxas_version == "roxas") {
  meas_created_at_converted <- lubridate::parse_date_time(
    df_settings$meas_created_at,
    orders = settings_date_orders,
    tz = Sys.timezone()
  )
  df_settings$meas_created_at <- meas_created_at_converted
}
```

Combine the extracted data into one object:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
rxs_images <- build_QWAimages(df_structure, df_settings)
rm(df_structure, df_settings)

rxs_images  # prints a summary of the image-level metadata
```

`rxs_images` is a `QWAimages` object: a tibble subclass holding the
per-image metadata (file paths, image EXIF data, and ROXAS settings),
with the `roxas_version` stored as an attribute. It can be saved to a
compressed CSV for later use:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write_QWAimages(rxs_images, "path/to/output_data/example_dataset_QWAimages.csv.gz")
# rxs_images <- read_QWAimages("path/to/output_data/example_dataset_QWAimages.csv.gz")
```

## Additional metadata for TRIA submission (Step 3b)

To provide the site-, tree-, woodpiece-, slide-, and dataset-level
metadata required for a TRIA submission, use the interactive metadata
Shiny app. It takes a `QWAimages` object as its starting point and
guides you through filling in the required fields. The output is a full
`QWAmetadata` object, which is exported as a `.json` file. Partially
completed submissions can be reloaded and continued at any time.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
launch_metadata_app()

# After exporting and closing the app, optionally read the result back:
# QWA_meta <- read_QWAmetadata("path/to/output_data/example_dataset_QWAmetadata.json")
```

See `vignette("metadata-app")` for a full walkthrough of the app.

---

# Step 4: Read and clean the measurement data

`collect_raw_data()` reads the cell and ring measurement tables from all
ROXAS output files, combines them, and performs initial cleaning:
negative values and error codes are replaced with `NA`, the dating is
checked for gaps or future years, and a warning is issued if CWT
estimates appear to be missing (relevant for conifer data).

`complete_QWAdata()` then adds derived cell and ring measures (e.g. total
cell area, relative wall thickness, cell diameters, earlywood/latewood
classification and widths) and computes ring quality flags:

- `incomplete_ring`: ring at the inner or outer image border where the
  true ring boundary is not visible; MRW is unreliable or unavailable.
- `missing_ring`: no cells detected; ring was added manually during
  crossdating (typically a wedging ring).
- `duplicate_ring`: the same year appears in more than one image due to
  overlapping slides from the same woodpiece.
- `exclude_dupl`: `TRUE` for the duplicate ring(s) not selected as the
  preferred source (ranked by cell count, penalising incomplete and
  missing rings).
- `exclude_issues`: rings to exclude from analyses, initialised from
  `incomplete_ring`. Missing rings are not excluded, as their zero width
  is a valid measurement; set `exclude_issues` afterwards to use a
  different rule.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
QWA_data <- collect_raw_data(rxs_images)
# or if you already loaded the full metadata from json after completing Step 3:
# QWA_data <- collect_raw_data(QWA_meta$images)

QWA_data <- complete_QWAdata(QWA_data, rxs_images)
# to also exclude missing rings:
# QWA_data$rings$exclude_issues <- QWA_data$rings$incomplete_ring | QWA_data$rings$missing_ring

QWA_data  # prints an overview including ring flag counts
```

---

# Step 5: Save the QWA data

`write_QWAdata()` saves the `QWAdata` object to two (optionally
compressed) CSV files following the naming convention
`{dataset_name}_QWAcells.csv(.gz)` and
`{dataset_name}_QWArings.csv(.gz)`. Explicit file names can also
be provided (see `?write_QWAdata`).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
path_out <- "path/to/output_data"
dataset_name <- "example_dataset"
write_QWAdata(QWA_data, dir = path_out, dataset_name = dataset_name)

# QWA_data <- read_QWAdata(dir = path_out, dataset_name = dataset_name)
```

At this stage you have the minimal components required for a TRIA
submission: the `QWAmetadata` `.json` file (from Step 3b) and the two
`QWAdata` `.csv` files. The following steps are optional but recommended
for a more complete submission.

---

# Step 6: Assess the measurements data quality (optional)

## Compute radial profiles (Step 6a)

Cell measurements can be aggregated across the ring width into
position bins, producing a `QWAprofile` object. Two binning schemes are
available:

- **Sector profiles**: divide each ring into *n* bins of equal *relative*
  width (0–100% of ring width). Comparable across rings of different
  absolute widths.
- **Band profiles**: sliding window of fixed *absolute* width and step
  size (in µm). Meaningful when absolute radial position matters (e.g.
  density gradients in µm from the cambium).

Both support computing means and optional quantiles per bin. With
`apply_exclusions = TRUE`, the cells of excluded rings (`exclude_dupl`,
`exclude_issues`) are removed before aggregating; `tissue = "affected"`
removes only the earlywood or latewood cells of rings whose
`affected_tissue` is `"ew"` or `"lw"`. Use these after flagging rings in
Step 6b.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
prf_sector <- calculate_sector_profiles(QWA_data,
                                        n_sectors = 5,
                                        sel_cell_params = c("la", "cwttan"),
                                        quant_probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))

# prf_band <- calculate_band_profiles(QWA_data,
#                                     bandwidth = 50, stepsize = 25,
#                                     sel_cell_params = c("la", "cwttan"),
#                                     quant_probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))

# After flagging rings (Step 6b), recalculate with exclusions applied:
# prf_sector <- calculate_sector_profiles(QWA_data, n_sectors = 5,
#                                         sel_cell_params = c("la", "cwttan"),
#                                         apply_exclusions = TRUE, tissue = "affected")

# Save and reload:
# write_QWAprofile(prf_sector, "path/to/output_data/example_dataset_QWAprofile_sector5.csv.gz")
# prf_sector <- read_QWAprofile("path/to/output_data/example_dataset_QWAprofile_sector5.csv.gz")
```

---

## Visualise measurement series and flag rings (Step 6b)

The flags Shiny app provides an interactive overview of the ring
measurements and allows you to annotate individual rings with data
quality flags (e.g. compression wood, cracks) and discrete feature
flags (e.g. blue rings, frost rings).

The app takes as input (loaded from file or from the current R
environment):

- The `$rings` component of a `QWAdata` object (required).
- A sector `QWAprofile` (optional) — plotted alongside the ring
  time series to aid visual inspection.
- A `QWAimages` object (optional) — used to display image-level
  comments and to allow opening image files directly from the app.

The output is the `QWAdata$rings` data frame with additional columns
for the flags, `comment` and `affected_tissue`. If image-level comments
were reviewed, the app also saves the image metadata with the
`comment_handled` column. The rings can be saved to file and read back to
update the `QWAdata` object:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
launch_flags_app()

# To update QWA_data$rings with the edited output:
# QWA_data$rings <- read_QWAdata(
#   file_rings = "path/to/output_data/example_dataset_edited_QWArings.csv")$rings
# QWA_data$rings <- df_rings_edited  # or directly from a data frame in the env
# write_QWAdata(QWA_data, dir = path_out, dataset_name = dataset_name, overwrite = TRUE)
```

`extract_ring_measures()` returns the ring measurements without the
excluded rings, as input for further analyses:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df_meas <- extract_ring_measures(QWA_data$rings)
```

See `vignette("flags-app")` for a full walkthrough of the app.

---

## Update images (Step 6c)

`update_QWAdata()` synchronises a `QWAdata` object with a `QWAimages`
object: images new in `rxs_images` are read and added, images no longer
in `rxs_images` are removed, and images listed in `imgs_to_reread` are
read again from their raw data files. This avoids reprocessing the
entire dataset. Duplicate-ring flags are recalculated for all
woodpiece-years affected by these changes. Added and re-read images are
new data: inspect their flags again (Step 6b) or re-apply any custom
rule for `exclude_issues`.

### Re-analysed images

If data processing reveals issues in the raw data and you re-analyse
one or more images with ROXAS or ROXAS AI:

1. Replace the output files in `path_in` with the newly generated files.
2. Re-read the settings/metadata for those images in the `QWAimages`
   object (no need to repeat Steps 1 and 2):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rxs_images <- update_QWAimages(rxs_images,
  imgs_to_reread = c("IMAGELABEL1", "IMAGELABEL2"),
  settings_date_orders = settings_date_orders) # same as defined in Step 3
# if a QWAmetadata object exists, update it as well (keeps the values
# entered in the metadata app):
# QWA_meta <- update_QWAmetadata(QWA_meta, rxs_images)
```

3. Update the `QWAdata` object. For the re-read images, derived measures
   and automatic flags are recalculated. By default, any manual edits
   made in the flags app for these images are also reset. Set
   `reset_manual_flags = FALSE` to keep them only if the re-analysis was
   minor and the dating was not affected:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
QWA_data <- update_QWAdata(QWA_data, meta = rxs_images,
  imgs_to_reread = c("IMAGELABEL1", "IMAGELABEL2"))
```

4. Review `only_ew` and `img_comment` of the re-analysed images in the
   metadata app, e.g. a comment noting that the image needs re-analysis.

### Added or removed images

To add images, there are two options:

- Rerun Steps 1--3 on the updated `path_in` to rebuild `rxs_images`.
  Any `only_ew` and `img_comment` values entered in the metadata app
  are then missing from `rxs_images` (`update_QWAmetadata()` below
  fills them in).
- Run Steps 1--3 on a separate folder containing only the new images to
  obtain `rxs_images_new`, and combine it with the existing object. This
  keeps existing values. Both objects must have the same ROXAS version
  and distinct image labels:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rxs_images <- combine_QWAimages(rxs_images, rxs_images_new)
```

To remove images, filter them from `rxs_images`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rxs_images <- rxs_images |>
  dplyr::filter(!image_label %in% c("IMAGELABEL1", "IMAGELABEL2"))
```

Then update the `QWAdata` object:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
QWA_data <- update_QWAdata(QWA_data, meta = rxs_images)
```

If a `QWAmetadata` object exists, update it as well. This replaces its
images and adds or removes the corresponding rows (and updates the
counts) in the sites, trees, woodpieces and slides tables, keeping the
existing metadata. Any `only_ew` and `img_comment` values missing or
`NA` in `rxs_images` are filled from `QWA_meta$images`, so this also
recovers them after a rebuild. Complete any added rows in the metadata
app.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
QWA_meta <- update_QWAmetadata(QWA_meta, rxs_images)
```

### Combining datasets

Two datasets prepared separately, e.g. from different input folders, can
be combined with `combine_QWAimages()`, `combine_QWAdata()` and
`combine_QWAmetadata()`. Both must have the same ROXAS version and
distinct image labels. Where both contain the same entry (e.g. a shared
site or author), the first object takes precedence. Duplicate-ring flags
are recalculated for woodpiece-years with rings from both datasets.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rxs_images <- combine_QWAimages(rxs_images_1, rxs_images_2)
QWA_data <- combine_QWAdata(QWA_data_1, QWA_data_2)
QWA_meta <- combine_QWAmetadata(QWA_meta_1, QWA_meta_2)
```

After any of these updates, save the data again:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write_QWAdata(QWA_data, dir = path_out, dataset_name = dataset_name, overwrite = TRUE)
```

---

# Step 7: Compile supplementary files (optional)

A TRIA submission must include at minimum the `QWAmetadata` `.json` and
the `QWAdata` `.csv(.gz)` files. If you want to provide additional
(supplementary) files (original images, annotated images, raw ROXAS /
ROXAS AI output, reference series `.rwl` files, etc.) these should be
submitted in a single zip alongside a standalone supplementary CSV
listing all the files in the zip.

Not all files may be eligible as supporting material for a TRIA dataset,
and it is important to track which file pertains to which image or slide,
etc. For this purpose, `compile_supplementary()` scans a directory (including
nested subfolders) and returns a table with one row per file it finds.
For each file it infers the `resource_type` from the file name and sets
the hierarchy level it belongs to (`linked_level`). Files are also
matched to their `linked_label` (e.g. the `image_label`) using a
`QWAimages` object, where possible.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
suppl_res <- compile_supplementary("path/to/supplementary_files", rxs_images = rxs_images)
# or rxs_images = QWA_meta$images
```

Every file gets a `status` (`"ok"`, `"review"`, or `"ignore"`) and the
console reports whether the supplementary path is ready for submission, 
or which files still need attention. Review the table, add a `description`
for files where the `resource_type` could not be inferred, and complete 
any `linked_label` values that were not filled automatically. Then
write it to a CSV to submit alongside the supplementary zip:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
suppl_res
vroom::vroom_write(suppl_res, "path/to/output_data/example_dataset_supplementary_files.csv",
                   delim = ",", na = "")
```

See `vignette("supplementary")` for more details on this step, including how
to `recompile_supplementary()` after making edits, and how to run a final
`check_supplementary()` once you are done.

# Step 8: Submit your data

Once you are ready to share your prepared data files with us, email
[tria@wsl.ch](mailto:tria@wsl.ch)---either with a link to the files on a
file transfer service of your choice, or asking for an invite link to
WSL's own one. See `vignette("submission")` for what to upload and what
happens to your files once we receive them.
